rewriteLast.title: Chapter 3 · The Flitting of the Fairies
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a line of small folk in green and grey carrying tiny bundles and lanterns across a moonlit marsh of tall grass and silver dykes, an old country woman at her cottage door holding a sleeping baby and watching them go, low mist, soft blue and silver moonlight

blocks.text: The next tale came from a farm worker of the old Marsh, who had it from his grandmother's grandmother. It happened in the days of good Queen Bess. She was the queen in whose time the great playwright wrote his plays for all the people of England.
The little folk carrying their lanterns across the Marsh, under the moon.

For hundreds of years the fairies had lived on Romney Marsh, in the wool-pits and under the thorns. They danced by the silver dykes, and no one troubled them. But a new parson came who did not like old ways. The church walls were whitewashed, and the quiet marks of the little folk were painted over. So they said to one another, 'It is time to flit.'
To 'flit' is an old word for moving house. The fairies do not leave in anger — they leave politely, because the world above ground is changing. And they thank the friends who were kind to them.

So they made ready very quietly, packing their little goods and glimmering lanterns, meaning to cross the sea to France, where old ways were still welcome. One old woman of the Marsh had been kind to them all her life. She stood at her door and watched them go by in the moonlight, with their bundles on their backs. And she called out a good-night to them.

The oldest fairy stopped and told her that kindness is never forgotten, wherever little folk flit. Then the lanterns went out across the dykes, one by one, like stars setting into the sea. 'Do they all leave England, then?' Una asked, when the tale was done. 'Not all,' said Puck, smiling in the fern-shadow. Some stayed behind, hidden and harmless, in quiet places like this hill. And to-morrow night I have older friends for you. They come from the days when Rome kept soldiers on this island.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 · The Centurion of the Thirtieth
chapters.artPrompt: a young Roman soldier in a bronze helmet and red cloak standing on a great grey stone wall running over grassy hills to a far sea, a friend beside him holding a legion standard, mist lying in the northern valleys, clear morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The next evening, when the oaks grew dusky, a soldier sat down quietly on the mossy root. 'I am Parnesius,' he said, 'a centurion of the Thirtieth Legion, of the army of Rome.' He said he was born in Britain, as his father was, and he loved this green island as his own.
Parnesius takes his first watch on the Great Wall, with his friend Pertinax.

As a boy he learned to ride and to use sword and spear. When he was grown, the Eagles sent him north to the Great Wall. He saw it first from the crest of a hill. Grey stone ran from sea to sea over the ridges, tower upon tower. 'It is the fence of Britain,' said the old soldier who rode with him. North of it lived the wild tribes of the hills. And beyond the cold sea came bolder enemies still, sea-rovers in winged helmets, hungry for land.
A centurion was an officer who led about eighty men. The Romans called Britain 'the Island' because it stood at the far edge of their great empire.

On the Wall Parnesius met another young officer, Pertinax, and they were friends before that first day was done. They walked the towers together and learned every stone of their stretch. 'A wall is only as strong as the men who watch it,' said Pertinax. 'Then let us be men worth watching,' said Parnesius, laughing. When the moon rose they took their first watch side by side, and the stars came out over the northern hills.

'Was it lonely, up there between the two seas?' Dan asked. 'Sometimes,' said Parnesius. 'But a soldier learns to be a friend to his comrade and to the weather too.' He smiled. 'And the strangest friends come out of the mist. But that is a tale for another evening, and Puck will give it you soon.'

chapters.title: Chapter 5 · On the Great Wall
chapters.artPrompt: a long Roman wall of grey stone climbing over windswept green hills between two distant seas, small watch towers with glowing signal fires, an old tribesman with painted skin and a short bow talking with a young Roman officer at a gate, cold blue evening with one warm firelight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: 'Tell us about the Picts,' said Dan, and Parnesius laughed and told. The Picts were the dark little people of the north, who knew every hole and heather-bush beyond the Wall. They could vanish into the bracken like mice, and Rome called them enemies. But the soldiers who watched the Wall knew better. Allo was one of them, and he was the best friend the Wall had.
Allo of the Picts comes to the Wall gate to trade news for bread.

An old man named Allo came often to the gate, with his short bow and his bright eyes. He traded news for bread, and he could smell a storm before the clouds were up. Parnesius gave him bread and salt, as friends do. 'Little soldier,' he would say, 'the wind is changing. The Winged Hats are gathering on the sea, and they mean to land this summer. See that your towers are ready.'
The Winged Hats were sea-rovers from beyond the northern sea — bold sailors in helmets with wings, whose far grandsons would one day be called Vikings.

The garrison on the Wall was thin. The best legions had sailed away with a great general who wished to make himself Emperor. So the two friends made the Wall strong in other ways. They mended the towers, drilled their men, and learned every bird-call on the ridge. Nothing could cross unseen, by day or by night. It was hard, patient work, and it made the days go kindly.

Winter came, with deep snow on the hills and wolves crying in the valleys. Still the Wall stood, and the watch-fires burned orange against the dark. 'We are the fence of Britain,' said Pertinax, as they walked the rounds. 'And a fence holds best,' said Parnesius, 'when it holds quietly.' But far out on the grey water, sails were being made ready.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · The Winged Hats
chapters.artPrompt: two young Roman officers standing firm with shields at a stone gatehouse on a windy wall while striped-sail ships land warriors on the shore below, signal fires blazing along the towers at dusk, stormy blue clouds with warm fire glow, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Then came the year when the Winged Hats landed. They were tall men in winged helmets, with striped sails and painted shields. They came ashore in hundreds, hungry and bold. They did not come only to steal, said Allo. Their own seas were cold and hard, and they wanted land to live on.
The Winged Hats come ashore, and the signal fires run along the Wall.

Parnesius and Pertinax had few men, so they used the Wall itself for a weapon. The towers flared their fires from hill to hill till the whole ridge glowed. The news ran from fort to fort, as fast as fire could speak: 'The sea-rovers are here. Stand fast.' Every man stood to his post, and no one trembled.
A signal fire is a fire lit on a high place, so that people far away can see it. Long before telephones, fires and trumpets carried the news.

There was hard fighting at the gates, and the two friends were always where the push was heaviest. The sea-rovers were brave enemies, and the soldiers knew it, but the Wall would not break. Day after day it held. At last the sea-rovers saw that strength alone would never win. Allo carried words of peace between the two sides, for both trusted the old man.

So peace was made, and it was a wise peace. The Winged Hats were given good land, and they put down their swords and took up the plough. 'Remember this,' said Parnesius, smiling. 'The fierce sailors of that day became farmers, and their children's children are the English of to-day.' He stayed in Britain all his days, for he loved the island as his own, and Pertinax and he were friends to the end. Puck nodded, as if he had seen it all himself.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Young Men at the Manor
chapters.artPrompt: a young man in a green tunic sitting by a roaring fire in a great timber hall, a kind old woman in a shawl handing him a bowl of milk, hawks sleeping on perches by the door, long warm shadows on wooden walls, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One evening Puck brought a young man in a green tunic, and the children knew his face at once. 'I am Richard,' he said, 'son of Sir Hugh, who told you of the sword of Weland.' The sword was his now. And this was the tale of how he was tested when he was young.
Richard, a guest in the hall of the men of the Wolds, shares their supper.

When Richard was young, he went hawking one morning beyond the marshes, chasing his falcon over the high downs. Riders met him there — men of the old Danish blood, who dwelt far off beyond the Wolds. Their families and his had been at feud for years. They carried Richard off, falcon and all.
A feud is a quarrel between two families that lasts for years. Richard's captors were grandsons of the Danes who had settled in England long before the Normans came.

But they did not use him cruelly. He was kept at their great timber hall as an honoured guest, and no door was shut against him. The old mother of the house was kind to him, and taught him their songs and their speech. He ate at their board, and their dogs slept by his feet. Little by little Richard saw that they loved their land and their children just as his own people did.

In time the quarrel was made up, and Richard rode home. His father met him at the gate with tears in his eyes. 'I went away a Norman,' said Richard, 'and came back something better — an Englishman.' For the Norman and the Saxon and the Dane were kneading into one dough, and the loaf was England. He hung the sword of Weland above his door. It shines there to this day, if you know where to look.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Treasure and the Law
chapters.artPrompt: a wise bearded man in a long dark robe and round cap standing in a candlelit stone room, a great glittering diamond on a wooden table among heavy ledgers and gold coins, a tall window showing old London towers, deep warm candle glow, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The last visitor came quietly, like a man used to waiting. 'I am Kadmiel,' he said, 'of the Jews of London, in the days of King John.' He said the children had heard much of swords. Now they would hear of treasure — and of something better than treasure.
Kadmiel, keeper of his people's treasure, with the great diamond on his table.

In those days the Jews of England kept and lent the King's money. A great diamond came to Kadmiel's people, carried over the sea. It was a stone so bright that men did terrible things to win it. Kadmiel saw the blood that followed it from hand to hand, and he made up his mind.
In the Middle Ages, kings often borrowed from Jewish families, because other folk were not allowed to lend money for profit. It made the Jews rich — and unsafe.

'So I threw the diamond into the sea,' said Kadmiel, 'and let the water keep it. No man has died for it since.' He said a stone that breeds blood is not treasure at all. The sea can hold a secret better than any man.

Then he told them of the Law. Bad King John had ground the land till the Barons rose against him. They made the King set his seal to the Great Charter at Runnymede. It was the Law that says even a King must obey. 'Our treasure helped to buy that day,' said Kadmiel. 'And a Law like that is the one treasure that grows by being shared.'

The moon was high now, and the ferns stood silver in it. 'People come and people go,' said Puck, cheerfully, 'but the Old Things remember.' The smith and the mason, the soldier and the squire, the keeper of the Law. They are all here on Pook's Hill, for those who know how to look. Dan and Una walked home in the warm dark. They talked of swords and walls and diamonds, and of the Law that stands over kings.
